source.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Channels in Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Robin Hesse; Jonas Fischer; Simone Schaub-Meyer; Stefan Roth

page_placements.theme: Polysemantic neurons can be split into more monosemantic components (upstream inputs, weights, downstream paths)

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether CNN channels respond to multiple distinct concepts using class relevance, activation analysis, and a channel-disentangling intervention rather than the original sources’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports qualitative activation and feature-visualization results for channel #1660 and aggregate activation results after disentangling. ARV cosine similarity and the selected thresholds are used to identify or define candidate channels, so they are not recorded as outcome rows. The paper does not report a predictive-accuracy result.
record.test_reason: The paper uses an attribution-based criterion to find ResNet-50 channels strongly activated by two unrelated ImageNet classes. Its illustrative channel #1660 (digital clock and cauliflower) bears on V1 in a modern convnet. The rest of the results evaluate the authors' own disentangling method rather than how often or how strongly polysemanticity occurs.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present a proof-of-concept tool that identifies γ-polysemantic channels (a class-based definition) and splits them into channels each activating for one concept. They note that the hyperparameters are handpicked and the method may work best in later layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses post-hoc weight restructuring to create explicit channels for two concepts in a pretrained CNN. It does not reproduce the original sources’ methods.
record.method_sensitivity: No outcome sensitivity comparison is reported. The authors state that τ, γ, and p are handpicked and application-specific; experiments focus on the last convolutional layer and two-concept disentanglement.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected γ-polysemantic channels can be split, via distinct previous-layer inputs, into two channels. Across the selected channels, these keep 114%/125% of the original activation for their own class and −9%/−21% for the other; the residual channel is about 0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The concepts mixed in a polysemantic CNN channel draw on largely separate upstream channels and can be explicitly separated without changing the network output.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), The First Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability for Vision (MIV)
record.problems: Evidence is limited to one qualitative channel example and aggregate activation values for selected channels. Polysemanticity is defined using class labels and thresholds; the authors note the formulation may work better in later layers. No control comparison, uncertainty estimate, or measured predictive-performance result is reported.
record.rows_left_out: The ARV cosine similarity of 0.47 for channel #1660 and the relevance/polysemanticity thresholds are used to select or define candidate channels, not reported as outcome measures.

untested.parts: Only one illustrative channel (#1660) is shown, in the last conv layer of ResNet-50. The number or share of γ-polysemantic channels is not reported.
Superposition is cited as a possible cause but not tested.
No comparison across architectures, activation functions or regularization.

No test of whether the clock/cauliflower mixture shares a feature. Some cauliflower patterns remain in the clock channel's visualization. Unrelatedness is assumed via ARV similarity below 0.5 and a WordNet proxy.
Thresholds τ, γ and p are handpicked. Outcomes under other thresholds are not reported.

record.verdict_notes: V6 was relabelled from 'challenges' to untested. The paper's ARV and WordNet criteria select pairs presumed unrelated; they do not test whether a shared feature exists. The total count of polysemantic channels found is not reported anywhere in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Only a ResNet-50 penultimate convolutional layer is studied; the qualitative example is channel #1660, and the quantitative results aggregate over selected polysemantic channels.
No transformer language models or language-model neurons are studied.
Superposition is discussed as a possible explanation, but the study does not test whether capacity pressure causes the observed mixtures.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.
No activation-function, architecture, or regularization comparison is made. The study does not report predictive performance after disentanglement.
The paper examines a selected CNN channel and class-based concepts, not a representative set of canonical neurons or a broad test of whether their mixtures share a feature.
The study does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods. It notes that its thresholds are application-specific but does not measure outcome changes across them.

labels.reason: R1 and R2: the channel is most strongly activated by both classes, and its MACO visualization shows both concepts. This is one hand-picked unit and gives no prevalence.

relation.reason: Its own results (channel #1660 identified as gamma-polysemantic, with top images and MACO showing both concepts) bear on whether V1 holds in ResNet-50. The evidence is thin but the relation is tests.

tranche.reason: The study finds polysemantic channels in ResNet-50 with its own method (class attribution plus ARV cosine) and shows channel #1660 with top patches and MACO. That is a different method aimed at the V1 question. Because it reports evidence beyond its own method's performance, it is not T4.

source_check.notes: Section 4 says 'penultimate layer' and the appendix says 'last convolutional layer'; in ResNet-50 these are the same layer. R3-R11 evaluate the authors' own method and are correctly left unlinked. The number of gamma-polysemantic channels is never stated, and Figure 4 (WordNet vs ARV similarity) is figure-only. Hyperparameters (tau 0.03, p 0.75, gamma 0.5) are handpicked, and the definition is class-based only.

statements.correction: Text: in ImageNet-trained ResNet-50, last conv layer, channel #1660 is most strongly activated by digital clock and cauliflower images alike, and its MACO visualization shows both. ARV cosine 0.47 (not cited). 'Unrelated' is the authors' judgment. CVPRW 2025 (MIV workshop), code given.

Mean relative activation over all gamma-polysemantic channels in ResNet-50's last conv layer: Disentangled 1 is 114% (concept 1) and -9% (concept 2). Disentangled 2 is -21% (concept 1) and 125% (concept 2). Residual is about 0%.
statements.problem: 'Selected' is loose. Table 1 is a mean over all gamma-polysemantic channels (gamma=0.5) in ResNet-50's last conv layer, using only images where the channel's relative attribution exceeds tau. Each channel is split into two concept channels plus a residual channel.
